hook.situation: A class event needs chairs, drinks, guide books, paper, and even a dog coming with a student. In Korean, each of those quantities needs the right counter.
objectives: Use noun + number + counter order confidently.
Pick the common counter for people, animals, things, cups, books, sheets, clothing sets, machines, and occurrences.
Use the changed native number forms 한, 두, 세, 네, and 스무 before counters.
hook.whyItMatters: English can say 'three students, two coffees, ten papers' with almost no classifier changes. Korean asks what kind of thing you are counting: people take 명, animals take 마리, drinks take 잔, books take 권, and flat sheets take 장.

grammarNotes.title: Basic order — noun + number + counter
grammarNotes.mentalModel: First name the thing, then count it with the correct counter: 학생 세 명, 커피 두 잔, 책 두 권.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun + native Korean number + counter is the default pattern for many everyday objects and people.

examples.en: I will prepare four cups of coffee.
Please give me just two books.
Ten sheets of paper are enough.

exceptions: The counter follows the number, not the noun directly: 책 두 권, not 책 권 두.
In speech, the noun can be omitted if it is already clear: 두 잔 주세요.

grammarNotes.title: Native number contractions — 하나 becomes 한
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Before counters, the first few native numbers shrink. This is why Koreans say 한 개 and 두 명, not 하나 개 and 둘 명.
grammarNotes.formation: 하나 → 한, 둘 → 두, 셋 → 세, 넷 → 네, 스물 → 스무 before a counter.

examples.en: They say they are bringing one dog too.

exceptions: 스물 becomes 스무 only before a counter: 스무 명, but 스물이에요 when standing alone.
Counters that use Sino-Korean labels, such as room or bus numbers, follow a different number system.

grammarNotes.title: People and animals — 명, 분, 마리
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Use 명 for people, 분 when you want to respectfully count people, and 마리 for animals.
grammarNotes.formation: Person noun + number + 명/분. Animal noun + number + 마리.

examples.note: 명 is the standard people counter.
Use 마리, not 명, for pets.

exceptions: Do not use 명 for animals.
분 can also mean minutes in other contexts; sentence meaning tells you whether it means people or minutes.

grammarNotes.title: Objects, drinks, books, and sheets — 개, 잔, 권, 장
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Generic things take 개, but common item types have their own counters that sound more natural.
grammarNotes.formation: Use 개 for general objects, 잔 for cups/glasses, 권 for books, and 장 for flat thin items such as paper, photos, or tickets.

examples.note: 개 is a safe general object counter.
장 counts flat items like photos and paper.

exceptions: 개 is understandable for many objects, but 책 두 개 sounds childish or object-like; 책 두 권 is natural.
장 is for flat thin items, not all physical objects.

grammarNotes.title: Sets and machines — 벌 and 대
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Some counters count a complete set or a machine rather than a loose object.
grammarNotes.formation: Use 벌 for a set of clothing and 대 for vehicles or machines.

examples.en: I packed only one set of clothes.

examples.note: 벌 fits suits or outfit sets.

exceptions: 차 can mean tea or car; context decides. Tea is counted with 잔, cars with 대.
For a single clothing item that is not a set, Koreans may use 개 or specific garment words, but 벌 is the useful beginner counter for outfits/suits.

grammarNotes.title: 번 — times, turns, or number labels
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 번 is flexible: it can count occurrences with native numbers, or label a number in a sequence with Sino-Korean numbers.
grammarNotes.formation: For occurrences, use native-style forms: 한 번, 두 번, 세 번. For labels, use Sino-Korean numbers: 일 번, 이 번, 삼 번.

examples.ko: 이 준비는 벌써 세 번 해 봤어요.
examples.romanization: i junbineun beolsseo se beon hae bwasseoyo.
examples.en: We have already done this prep three times.
Please explain it one more time.
examples.note: 한 번 means once or one time.
이 번 is a number label.

examples.en: How many times did you do it?
examples.note: 몇 번 asks about frequency or number, depending on context.

exceptions: 세 번 means three times; 삼 번 usually means number three.
첫 번째 / 두 번째 / 세 번째 is the ordinal pattern for first, second, third.

exampleSentence.en: They say they are bringing one dog too.
I will prepare four cups of coffee.
Please give me just two guide books too.
Ten sheets of paper are enough.
I packed only one set of clothes.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two staff members prepare supplies for a small trial class.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 오늘 체험 수업에 학생 몇 명 와요?
lines.romanization: oneul cheheom sueobe haksaeng myeot myeong wayo?
lines.en: How many students are coming to today's trial class?
lines.grammarNote: 명 counts people; 몇 명 asks how many people.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 학생 세 명이 오고, 강아지 한 마리도 데려온대요.
lines.romanization: haksaeng se myeongi ogo, gangaji han marido deryeondaeyo.
lines.en: Three students are coming, and they say they are bringing one dog too.
lines.grammarNote: 세 명 for people; 한 마리 for an animal.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 그럼 의자 네 개랑 커피 네 잔 준비할게요.
lines.romanization: geureom uija ne gaerang keopi ne jan junbihalgeyo.
lines.en: Then I will prepare four chairs and four cups of coffee.
lines.grammarNote: 개 counts chairs; 잔 counts cups of coffee.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: How many sheets of paper do we need?
lines.grammarNote: 장 counts flat sheets such as paper, photos, and tickets.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 열 장이면 돼요. 안내 책도 두 권만 주세요.
lines.romanization: yeol jangimyeon dwaeyo. annae chaekdo du gwonman juseyo.
lines.en: Ten sheets are enough. Please give me just two guide books too.
lines.grammarNote: 권 counts books; 장 counts paper sheets.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 이 준비는 벌써 세 번 해 봐서 괜찮아요.
lines.romanization: i junbineun beolsseo se beon hae bwaseo gwaenchanayo.
lines.en: We have already done this prep three times, so it is fine.

readingText.title: 몇 개가 아니라 무엇을 세는지 먼저 보기
readingText.body: 한국어에서 수량을 말할 때는 숫자만 맞으면 끝이 아니에요. 무엇을 세는지 먼저 봐야 해요. 학생은 세 명, 강아지는 한 마리, 커피는 네 잔, 책은 두 권, 종이는 열 장처럼 명사에 맞는 단위가 달라져요. 처음에는 개를 모든 물건에 붙이고 싶지만, 책 두 개보다 책 두 권이 자연스럽고, 사진 세 개보다 사진 세 장이 자연스러워요. 또 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷은 단위명사 앞에서 한, 두, 세, 네로 줄어들어요. 그래서 하나 명이 아니라 한 명, 둘 잔이 아니라 두 잔이라고 말해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: In Korean, counting is not only about choosing the right number. You first look at what kind of thing you are counting. Students are counted with 명, animals with 마리, cups of coffee with 잔, books with 권, and sheets of paper or photos with 장. The first few native Korean numbers also contract before counters: 하나 becomes 한, 둘 becomes 두, 셋 becomes 세, and 넷 becomes 네.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 학생을 셀 때 어떤 단위명사를 써요?
책 두 개보다 어떤 표현이 더 자연스러워요?
하나, 둘, 셋, 넷은 단위명사 앞에서 어떻게 바뀌어요?

culturalNote.title: Using 개 for everything sounds beginner-like
culturalNote.body: 개 is useful and often understood, but Korean speakers use more specific counters whenever they are common. 책 두 개, 사진 세 개, 커피 두 개 may be understood, but 책 두 권, 사진 세 장, 커피 두 잔 sound much more natural. In service settings, using the right counter also makes requests clearer.
culturalNote.tip: When you learn a new noun, learn one counting chunk with it: 책 한 권, 커피 한 잔, 사진 한 장, 강아지 한 마리.

inlineExercises.explanation: 장 counts flat sheets such as paper.
번 counts occurrences or number labels depending on context.

bullets: Basic order: noun + number + counter, as in 학생 세 명 and 커피 두 잔.
Native number contractions: 한, 두, 세, 네, 스무 before counters.
People and animals: 명/분 for people, 마리 for animals.
Objects and formats: 개 for general things, 잔 for drinks, 권 for books, 장 for flat sheets.
Sets and machines: 벌 for clothing sets, 대 for vehicles and machines.
번 can mean times or number labels: 세 번 vs 삼 번.
